analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending and donations, curbs party soft money, and gives small donors a tax credit.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in any of the four committees it was sent to, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a voluntary spending cap of $600,000 for House campaigns, with candidates who accepted the cap getting benefits in return: a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 per couple) for small contributions, discounted TV airtime, and cheap nonprofit-rate campaign mail. It capped contributions from big donors and political committees at $300,000 per candidate, banned national parties from raising unrestricted 'soft money' for federal races, required broadcasters to sell candidates ad time at their lowest rate with no preemption, and imposed tighter reporting and audit rules on campaign money. It also barred federal candidates from repaying personal loans with post-election donations and banned 'leadership' PACs run by officeholders.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and small donors: the tax credit would let ordinary people fund campaigns on equal footing with large donors, and candidates accepting the limits would rely on many small gifts rather than a few large ones. Challengers benefit because spending caps shrink incumbents' money advantage, and the bill forces incumbents with more than $600,000 on hand to move the excess out of their campaign accounts. Closed-captioning requirements and the debate requirement for presidential candidates who take public funds would also serve viewers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, small donors, and House challengers

how_it_helps.text: Gives a tax credit of up to $100 per individual ($200 joint) for contributions to participating House candidates, encouraging small donations [S2][S3].
Caps participating House candidates at $600,000 in spending and $600,000 in contributions per election cycle, and limits political committee and large-donor contributions to $300,000 [S2][S3].
Requires incumbents holding more than $600,000 in campaign funds to move the excess out of their re-election account, reducing the built-in advantage of officeholders [S3].

Bans national party committees from soliciting or accepting contributions not subject to federal limits, and subjects party spending that touches federal elections to federal limits and reporting [S2][S3].
Requires broadcasters to provide candidates airtime at the lowest charge and bars them from preempting candidate ads, and extends nonprofit-rate mailing to eligible House candidates [S2][S3].

Strengthens enforcement by letting the FEC seek court injunctions against ongoing violations and conduct random audits, and requires 'stand by your ad'-style disclosure statements in campaign advertising [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, political committees, and parties that used unrestricted money to influence federal elections would lose that channel. Incumbents with large war chests would see their advantage trimmed. Broadcasters would lose revenue by selling candidate airtime at deep discounts and losing preemption flexibility. The tax credit and postal subsidy would cost federal revenue, which the bill addressed by requiring budget neutrality and offsets elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: Spending limits on campaign expenditures conflict with the Supreme Court's Buckley v. Valeo ruling that campaign spending is protected speech; the bill anticipated this by providing expedited Supreme Court review and declaring the entire act invalid if its core spending-limit title falls [S3].
The tax credit and below-cost mailing and broadcast rates are public subsidies for campaigns; even with a budget-neutrality requirement, they shift resources toward political advertising [S2][S3].

The bill tightens rules on parties and nonparticipating candidates (cutting their contribution limits to $500 per person), which could pressure candidates into the public system and tilt rules toward the two major parties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was an ambitious attempt to curb big money in House races and offset the burden on candidates with subsidies and discounted airtime. Its main risk was constitutional: mandatory-style spending limits had already been struck down by the Supreme Court, and the bill's own severability clause conceded that its centerpiece might not survive. Its administrative complexity, spread across four committees, also made it harder to move than narrower reforms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees on the day it was introduced, two subcommittees took referrals, and no committee ever acted on it, so it never came up for a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Glen Browder introduced the Fair Campaign Finance Reform Act of 1993 on May 20, 1993, and it was referred the same day to four committees: House Administration, Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Post Office and Civil Service [S1][S3][S5].
In late May and early June 1993 it was referred to subcommittees on Postal Operations and Services and Telecommunications and Finance; the bill had zero cosponsors [S4][S5].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on September 30, 1993, and no further action was ever recorded; the bill died in committee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and their large donors were better off: no spending caps, no limits on big contributions or party soft money, and no requirement to disgorge large war chests ever took effect. Broadcasters also kept charging full rates for political ads.

for.name: Rep. Glen Browder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Charlie Rose
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or action on the bill in the committee with primary jurisdiction over campaign finance.

against.name: Chairs of the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Post Office and Civil Service Committees
against.role: Committee chairs (all Democrats) holding parallel referrals
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill in their committees during the 103rd Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan alignment can be measured; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and the Democratic-controlled committees took no action.

industries.note: The bill capped contributions from political committees and large individual donors at $300,000 per candidate and tightened rules on conduits and bundled giving. Their ability to bankroll House campaigns was the main target of the bill.

The bill barred national parties from raising unlimited 'soft money' for federal elections and subjected party spending that touches federal races to federal limits and reporting. Parties would have lost their main channel for unlimited money.

The bill required stations to sell candidate ads at the lowest charge (with a further 50% discount for participating candidates), barred preemption of candidate spots, and imposed ad-disclosure rules. Broadcasters profit from high-priced political advertising, so their interest ran against cheaper access for campaigns.

The bill forced incumbents with over $600,000 banked to move the excess out of their campaign accounts and capped spending and fundraising for participants, trimming the financial advantages of holding office. Officeholders as a class benefited from the bill never becoming law.
